text:
Florence Fennel.
DIFFICULTY
Medium
3/5
HARVEST SEASONS
Summer / Autumn

Florence fennel, or bulb fennel, is a sweet, aniseed-flavoured umbellifer grown for the swollen bases of its leaf-stalks. It belongs to the same broad family as carrot, parsnip and celeriac, but is eaten quite differently: sliced raw in salads, cooked gently for a soft creamy flavour, or used in soups and ratatouille. The feathery leaves are also edible, with a gentle aniseed flavour. Modern varieties have made it easier to grow by reducing the tendency to bolt before useful bulbs form. Match the variety to its sowing season and keep young plants growing steadily: drought, crowding or root checks can give stemmy plants instead of juicy bulbs. Summer sowings after an early crop are useful for autumn harvesting. Harvest while the bulbs are tender, before they become fibrous, stemmy or frosted.

Quick facts
Harvest

Jul – Oct

Sowing depth

5/8 in.

Row spacing

12 in. between rows

Plant spacing

12 in. for full bulbs, 6 in. for baby bulbs.

Yield (10 ft row)

About 10 full-size bulbs or 20 baby bulbs.

Sow

Jun–Jul outdoors. Use an early variety under cover in May.

Plant out

Late May–Jul, before roots fill the modules.

Ready in

From sowing: baby bulbs ~6 weeks; full bulbs 12–16 weeks

Recommended varieties
Zefa Fino

An established Florence fennel grown for swollen leaf bases. Keep growth steady with moisture and use appropriate sowing dates.

Romanesco

A traditional Florence fennel with substantial bulbs. Retain for gardeners who prefer a familiar non-hybrid selection.

Rondo F1

A modern Florence fennel producing rounded bulbs. A useful addition to the established open-pollinated choices.

Finale

Large, flattened bulbs with useful resistance to bolting.

Key risks
Bolting or stemmy bulbs

Cold while young, drought and root disturbance can trigger premature flowering.

Small or dry bulbs

Drought and poor fertility produce small, less juicy bulbs.

Lower sheath rot

Lower sheaths may soften and decay.

Frost

Hard frost damages bulbs.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
54
STALKS & SHOOTS

Keep growth steady and moist.

Drought, crowding and root disturbance can spoil bulb development.

Match sowing time to the variety.

Summer sowings usually give more reliable UK autumn bulbs.

Soil & preparation
Deep, fertile, moisture-retentive soil with plenty of humus gives tender, juicy bulbs.
Prepare with well-rotted manure or compost before sowing or planting. Avoid waterlogging.
A compost dressing about 2 in. deep, spread well before planting, feeds the crop and helps hold summer moisture.
Sowing & planting
Raise in modules
Plant level
Sow 

For the main crop, scatter seed thinly in the final bed. For an early crop, raise a suitable variety in modules under cover. Keep seedlings warm and growing steadily.

Plant out 

Move module plants while young. Keep the rootball intact and the growing point above soil level. Firm and water in.

Looking after the crop
Keep moisture even as bulbs swell: drought reduces juiciness and encourages bolting. Dress light or depleted soil with compost.
Hoe or hand-weed while plants are young: small plants compete poorly with weeds.
Thin direct-sown rows promptly. Crowded plants make smaller, less well-shaped bulbs and may run up to stem.
Earth up lightly where useful to keep the base tender and moist, without covering the growing centre or trapping rot around old sheaths.
Harvesting & storage
Cut tender bulbs before they turn fibrous or frost arrives: baby bulbs about 2 in. across, full bulbs about 4–6 in. Harvest elongating small bulbs promptly; they are unlikely to fatten.
Trim tough stems and use fronds for flavouring. Lift before hard frost; keep sound autumn bulbs cool and frost-free for short-term use.
If lower sheaths rot, lift promptly, discard rotten tissue and use only firm sound parts; discard extensively rotted bulbs.
Pests & diseases
Problem	What to look for	What to do
Bolting or stemmy bulbs	Small bulbs elongate or start flowering.	Harvest usable parts; match sowing dates to variety.
Small or dry bulbs	Bulbs stay small and lose juiciness.	Use compost, mulch and steady watering.
Lower sheath rot	Outer sheaths soften and decay.	Lift promptly; discard rot and use only sound tissue.
Frost	Bulbs deteriorate after freezing.	Harvest before hard frost; store sound bulbs frost-free.
Final tips

Raise modules as an early crop finishes; plant before roots become pot-bound.

Harvest stemmy bulbs promptly; they are unlikely to fatten later.

Compost mulch on light or depleted soil conserves summer moisture.

Pick for tenderness before frost, fibrous growth or decay; size alone is no guide.

VEGETABLE GUIDES
